item.title: Was Sleep Sacrificed in the Name of Clean Sport?
item.description:
Sleep

Was Sleep Sacrificed in the Name of Clean Sport?

What the Tour de France reveals about sleep, athletic performance, and policy.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Sleep is a biological necessity that public policy too often overlooks.
  • Even one night of disrupted sleep can impair attention, reaction time, and decision-making.
  • Good public policy shouldn't force a choice between achieving societal goals and protecting healthy sleep.

When people ask what I study, I explain that my work sits at the intersection of sleep science and public policy.

The typical response is, "Really? I never thought of sleep that way."

Most people think of sleep as a matter of personal responsibility

But over the past two decades, my work and that of many others has shown that some of the biggest threats to healthy sleep don't stop at the individual. They're built into the policies under which we live.

A friend of mine who follows professional cycling recently shared a story from the Tour de France that perfectly demonstrates this point.

Hours before Stage 15, two-time Tour de France champion Jonas Vingegaard was awakened at 2:00 a.m. by officials from the International Testing Agency (ITA) for a random anti-doping test. According to reports, the testing process lasted about 40 minutes, and Vingegaard later said it took him additional time to fall back asleep.

As a sleep scientist, that came as no surprise. Being awakened in the middle of the night, getting dressed, leaving your room, and providing a biological sample is hardly conducive to quickly falling back asleep. It is precisely the kind of disruption that makes returning to restorative sleep difficult.

During competition later that day, Vingegaard crashed, fracturing his collarbone and ending his Tour.

Did the disrupted sleep cause the crash?

Of course, we can't say that. Cycling crashes happen for many reasons. But as a sleep scientist, I think it raises an important question: What is gained by conducting a routine anti-doping test at 2:00 a.m. when decades of research tell us that disrupting sleep impairs reaction time, attention, decision-making, and motor coordination?

Why would we knowingly compromise one of the most fundamental biological contributors to performance?

And why would we do it in the context of one of the most physically and cognitively demanding sporting events in the world?

Sleep is not negotiable. It is one of the most powerful recovery tools athletes have. Even a single night of disrupted sleep slows reaction time, increases attentional lapses, impairs judgment, and reduces coordination. These are precisely the functions elite athletes depend on. In a sport like cycling, where split-second decisions can determine both performance and safety, these impairments matter enormously.

article continues after advertisement

None of this is an argument against anti-doping testing. Fair competition depends on it. But protecting clean sport should not come at the expense of healthy sleep. Good policy should protect both.

How sleep is discounted in public policy

This story resonated with me because it feels like yet another example of how easily sleep is discounted when it comes to public policy.

In fact, just last week, Congress passed the Sunshine Protection Act despite years of warnings from sleep and circadian scientists that permanent daylight saving time runs counter to human biology.

At first glance, these two events seem entirely unrelated. One involves elite cyclists. The other concerns our biological clocks.

But they share a common assumption: that sleep is somehow negotiable.

It isn't.

Whether we're talking about elite athletes, teenagers starting school before sunrise, physicians working overnight shifts, or U.S. citizens having to wake up in the dark of night in winter due to permanent daylight saving time, the lesson is the same: policies that ignore sleep ignore biology.

And biology always wins.

Sleep isn't a luxury. It isn't just downtime. It is a biological necessity and a performance imperative. It's time our policies started treating it that way.

item.title: In Praise of Boredom
item.description:
Boredom

In Praise of Boredom

Six ways to accomplish more by doing absolutely nothing.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Your least productive moments may be the ones in which your brain is doing its most important work.
  • Boredom creates the mental space needed for creativity, insight, and meaningful reflection.
  • Constant busyness and stimulation suppress curiosity and original thinking.

Dorothy Parker once observed, "The cure for boredom is curiosity. There is no cure for curiosity."

When was the last time you needed to be cured of boredom?

Today, being bored is as rare as hen’s teeth, as the British might say. In its place, we’ve substituted hyper-busyness: an endless to-do list nipping at our heels, emails demanding to be checked, podcasts filling in the gaps, social media tempting us to scroll just a tad longer, and calendars devoid of white space. We finish one thing and immediately jump to the next. Too often, we wear busyness as a badge of productivity. Yet we know that it's in the gaps between tasks and unstructured stillness that our most original thoughts take shape.

But what's the cost of that mindset? We've become experts at multitasking and eliminating the empty spaces in our day. Yet by filling every moment and choosing frenzy over focus, we forfeit something essential. We sacrifice the very condition our brains need to make unexpected connections, solve problems, and generate fresh ideas.

When our minds are constantly occupied by the relentless churn of “what next” and endless stimulation, there is little room for reflection, imagination, or the quiet mental wandering that gives birth to our best ideas. It’s only when we pause that our brains enter the default mode network, the state associated with reflection, memory, and creative insight. Here we retrieve memories, connect seemingly unrelated ideas, imagine future possibilities, and make meaning of our experiences. As Parker alluded, curiosity is the fruit of boredom. In these moments, when we appear to be doing nothing, our brains may actually be doing their most important work: thinking.

Are we inching closer to the world imagined in M.T. Anderson's dystopian novel Feed, where a constant stream of entertainment and information is fed directly into the mind, leaving little room for silence and reflection? Was this a harbinger of the world we are creating, one where curiosity withers, creativity struggles to take root, and we cease to think for ourselves?

If constant stimulation is the problem, perhaps being quiet is the antidote. We simply need to reclaim this way of being.

The Gift Hidden in Boredom

Boredom, or quiet time, isn't valuable because it's pleasant. In fact, many of us become anxious when bored and reach for the next distraction. Boredom is valuable because it creates the mental space from which creativity, insight, connection, and even purpose emerge. Doing nothing, often equated to being bored, is not wasted time. Rather, these quiet moments may be among the most productive of our day.

Perhaps that’s why childhood, prior to this era of constant connection and electronic noise, offered something many adults today rarely experience: long stretches of unstructured time. Like many children of the boomer generation, my summer days stretched endlessly before me. We rode bikes, invented games, and played with whatever neighborhood child wandered into our yard. And when alone, I would read, wonder, and write. There was always enough space to spark curiosity and to daydream.

article continues after advertisement

Today’s children often experience something different: days filled with organized activities and, in the spaces between them, screens. They have little time to be bored and little opportunity for the unstructured time that invites exploration and imagination. Are we doing ourselves or our children any favors by hyper-structuring every hour of the day?

The answer depends on the kind of boredom we’re talking about. Researchers increasingly distinguish between chronic boredom, which can undermine our well-being, and the temporary boredom that sparks imagination, curiosity, and creativity. Chronic boredom has been linked to depression, poor attention, loneliness, and risk-taking behaviors.

Temporary boredom is quite different. It is where the magic happens. It creates space for unexpected connections, creative problem-solving, and the “eureka” of new ideas that can only occur when our minds are free to wander. Some psychologists even suggest that this state can foster personal growth.

Lesson From an Airport

Years ago, during a delayed flight from Baltimore to Boston, I glanced up from my phone and saw that every single person was staring into a screen with glazed eyes. It was startling, and I was reminded of the era prior to cell phones, when delays could lead to conversations with strangers, at times sparking friendships, or even marriages.

So on that day, I put my phone away.

I began talking with another stranded traveler. Turns out he was a classical musician at Berklee College of Music. We spent the next hour talking about the risks of following a passion without a guaranteed income and the serendipity that shapes life's biggest decisions. I never saw him again, but I've never forgotten him or the conversation, something that would never have happened had I not looked away from the screen. It made me wonder how many conversations and special moments I've missed because I chose to look down instead of up.

article continues after advertisement

Making Room for Boredom

Here are some thoughts on how to make room for boredom:

Schedule time to be unscheduled. Set aside 30 minutes to do nothing. Look out the window, take a walk, or sit and let your mind wander.

Wait without reaching for your screen. Whether you're at an airport, in a waiting room, or standing in line, resist the urge to fill the silence. Truly see who is sitting across from you, and imagine their life story. Perhaps start a conversation.

Leave your phone behind. Go for a walk without a podcast, audiobook, or checking your messages. Take an unplanned route. See where your mind takes you.

Do a task that requires little thought. Organize a drawer, peel potatoes, or fold laundry. In her classic short story "I Stand Here Ironing," Tillie Olsen reminds us that simple, repetitive tasks often free the mind and make meaning.

Make room for awe. Read poetry. Sit on the porch. Watch, really watch, the birds. Wander through a museum. Let your mind drift, free from the pressure to accomplish anything.

Take a to-don’t day. Banish the list for one day. Then ask yourself, what do I really want to do, explore, or think about today?

In these empty moments, deep thought takes root, creativity flourishes, and curiosity awakens. Perhaps the next time boredom comes calling, invite it in.
